items.readable_text:
Content:
When considering an [MATH: m \times n] matrix [MATH: A] as a linear transformation

Content:
[MATH: \mathbb{R}^n \xrightarrow{\quad A \quad} \mathbb{R}^m,]

Content:
there are four fundamental subspaces that naturally occur. The first two are as follows:

Content:
- The column space of [MATH: A,] denoted [MATH: \text{Col}(A),] is a subspace of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^m.] This is the set of all linear combinations of the columns of [MATH: A.]
- The null space of [MATH: A,] denoted [MATH: \text{Null}(A),] is a subspace of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n.] This is the set of all vectors in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] that, when pre-multiplied by [MATH: A,] result in the zero-vector [MATH: \mathbf{0}.]

Content:
Now, notice that the transpose [MATH: A^T] is an [MATH: n \times m] matrix and can be considered as the transformation

Content:
[MATH: \mathbb{R}^m \xrightarrow{\quad A^T \quad} \mathbb{R}^n.]

Content:
So, we have similar subspaces for the transpose [MATH: A^T{:}]

Content:
- The column space of [MATH: A^T,] denoted [MATH: \text{Col}(A^T),] is a subspace of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n.] We call this the row space of [MATH: A] since the span of the columns of [MATH: A^T] is equivalent to the span of the rows of [MATH: A.]
- The null space of [MATH: A^T,] denoted [MATH: \text{Null}(A^T),] is a subspace of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^m.] We call this the left null space of [MATH: A] since it is equivalent to the set of all vectors [MATH: \mathbf y\in\mathbb R^m] such that [MATH: \mathbf y^T A = \mathbf{0}.]

Content:
Let's discuss how these spaces relate to each other:

Content:
- We have two subspaces in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] that are orthogonal complements of each other:
[MATH: \text{Col}(A^T) = \text{Null}(A)^\perp]
- We have two subspaces in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^m] that are orthogonal complements of each other:
[MATH: \text{Col}(A) = \text{Null}(A^T)^\perp]

Content:
The four fundamental subspaces of a matrix [MATH: A] can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b095df44e92efd16ab0a91bc3e09fc15]

Content:
To see why [MATH: \text{Col}(A)] is the orthogonal complement of [MATH: \text{Null}(A^T),] note the following:

Content:
- When calculating the product [MATH: A^T \mathbf x,] we multiply each row of [MATH: A^T] by [MATH: \mathbf x.]
- Suppose that [MATH: \mathbf x\in \text{Null}(A^T).] Then, by definition, [MATH: A^T \mathbf x = \mathbf 0.]
- Thus, [MATH: \mathbf x] must be orthogonal to each row of [MATH: A^T.] Equivalently, this means that [MATH: \mathbf x] is orthogonal to each column of [MATH: A.]
- Hence, [MATH: \text{Null}(A^T)] is orthogonal to [MATH: \text{Col}(A).]

Content:
We can deduce that [MATH: \text{Null}(A)] is the orthogonal complement of [MATH: \text{Col}(A^T)] by similar reasoning.

1. [MATH: \text{Null}(A)]
2. [MATH: \text{Col}(A)]
3. [MATH: \text{Null}(A^T)]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that [MATH: \text{Col}(A^T)] is the row space of [MATH: A,] and consists of all linear combinations of the rows of [MATH: A.]

If a vector is orthogonal to every linear combination of the rows of [MATH: A,] it must be orthogonal to each row of [MATH: A.] But notice that when pre-multiplying a vector by [MATH: A,] we multiply each row of [MATH: A] by that vector. So, [MATH: \text{Col}(A^T)] must be orthogonal to the null space of [MATH: A,] which is [MATH: \text{Null}(A).]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Note: In general, the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix [MATH: A] can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

items.readable_text:
Content:
Given an [MATH: m \times n] matrix [MATH: A,] what is the image of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] under [MATH: A?]

Content:
Note that pre-multiplying a vector [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n] by [MATH: A] gives a linear combination of the columns of [MATH: A{:}]
[MATH: [||||⋯||; a_{1}|a_{2}|⋯|a_{n};||||⋯||]]

Content:
Therefore, by definition, the image of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] under the action of [MATH: A] is [MATH: \text{Col}(A),] the column space of [MATH: A.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fd819e94aa13fdf60f90e01c4669cca7]

Content:
Similarly, pre-multiplying a vector [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^m] by [MATH: A^T] gives a linear combination of the columns of [MATH: A^T{:}]
[MATH: [||||⋯||; a_{1}^{T}|a_{2}^{T}|⋯|a_{m}^{T};||||⋯||]]

Content:
Therefore, the image of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^m] under the action of [MATH: A^T] must be [MATH: \text{Col}(A^T).] This is also the row space of [MATH: A,] since a linear combination of the columns of [MATH: A^T] is equivalent to a linear combination of the rows of [MATH: A.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/46bf86653ce6e6d460ef48eca5975949]

Content:
We can use similar reasoning to find the image of the four fundamental subspaces under the appropriate matrix.

items.title: Dimensions of the Four Fundamental Subspaces

sections.normalized_html: Consider an [MATH: m \times n] matrix [MATH: A] with rank [MATH: r.] The dimensions of the four fundamental subspaces of [MATH: A] are as follows:
sections.readable_text: Consider an [MATH: m \times n] matrix [MATH: A] with rank [MATH: r.] The dimensions of the four fundamental subspaces of [MATH: A] are as follows:

sections.normalized_html:
• [MATH: \text{dim}(\text{Col}(A)) = r.] Since the column space is the span of the columns of [MATH: A,] its dimension is the number of linearly independent columns which, by Gaussian elimination, is [MATH: \text{rank}(A)=r.]

  • [MATH: \text{dim}(\text{Col}(A^T)) = r.] It can be shown that the dimension of the row space of [MATH: A] also equals [MATH: r.] Therefore, [MATH: \text{rank}(A^T)=\text{rank}(A)=r.]

  • [MATH: \text{dim}(\text{Null}(A)) = n-r.] Since [MATH: \text{Null}(A)] is the orthogonal complement of [MATH: \text{Col}(A^T)] in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n,] we have that [MATH: \text{dim}(\text{Null}(A)) = \underbrace{\text{dim}(\mathbb{R}^n)}_{n} - \underbrace{\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A^T))}_{r} = n-r.]

Content:
If we consider an [MATH: m \times n] matrix [MATH: A] of rank [MATH: r] as a transformation from [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] to [MATH: \mathbb{R}^m,] then there are four fundamental subspaces of [MATH: A{:}]

Content:
- [MATH: \text{Col}(A)] and [MATH: \text{Null}(A^T)] are subspaces in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^m] with dimensions [MATH: r] and [MATH: m-r,] respectively.
- [MATH: \text{Col}(A^T)] and [MATH: \text{Null}(A)] are subspaces in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] with dimensions [MATH: r] and [MATH: n-r,] respectively.

Content:
Furthermore,

Content:
- [MATH: \text{Col}(A)] and [MATH: \text{Null}(A^T)] are orthogonal complements in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^m,] and
- [MATH: \text{Null}(A)] and [MATH: \text{Col}(A^T)] are orthogonal complements in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n.]

Content:
Finally, we have that

Content:
- the image of [MATH: \text{Col}(A^T)] under the action of [MATH: A] is [MATH: \text{Col}(A),] and
- the image of [MATH: \text{Col}(A)] under the action of [MATH: A^T] is [MATH: \text{Col}(A^T).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
When considering an [MATH: m \times n] matrix [MATH: A] as a linear transformation

Content:
[MATH: \mathbb{R}^n \xrightarrow{\quad A \quad} \mathbb{R}^m,]

Content:
there are four fundamental subspaces that naturally occur. The first two are as follows:

Content:
- The column space of [MATH: A,] denoted [MATH: \text{Col}(A),] is a subspace of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^m.] This is the set of all linear combinations of the columns of [MATH: A.]
- The null space of [MATH: A,] denoted [MATH: \text{Null}(A),] is a subspace of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n.] This is the set of all vectors in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] that, when pre-multiplied by [MATH: A,] result in the zero-vector [MATH: \mathbf{0}.]

Content:
Now, notice that the transpose [MATH: A^T] is an [MATH: n \times m] matrix and can be considered as the transformation

Content:
[MATH: \mathbb{R}^m \xrightarrow{\quad A^T \quad} \mathbb{R}^n.]

Content:
So, we have similar subspaces for the transpose [MATH: A^T{:}]

Content:
- The column space of [MATH: A^T,] denoted [MATH: \text{Col}(A^T),] is a subspace of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n.] We call this the row space of [MATH: A] since the span of the columns of [MATH: A^T] is equivalent to the span of the rows of [MATH: A.]
- The null space of [MATH: A^T,] denoted [MATH: \text{Null}(A^T),] is a subspace of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^m.] We call this the left null space of [MATH: A] since it is equivalent to the set of all vectors [MATH: \mathbf y\in\mathbb R^m] such that [MATH: \mathbf y^T A = \mathbf{0}.]

Content:
Let's discuss how these spaces relate to each other:

Content:
- We have two subspaces in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] that are orthogonal complements of each other:
[MATH: \text{Col}(A^T) = \text{Null}(A)^\perp]
- We have two subspaces in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^m] that are orthogonal complements of each other:
[MATH: \text{Col}(A) = \text{Null}(A^T)^\perp]

Content:
The four fundamental subspaces of a matrix [MATH: A] can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b095df44e92efd16ab0a91bc3e09fc15]

Content:
To see why [MATH: \text{Col}(A)] is the orthogonal complement of [MATH: \text{Null}(A^T),] note the following:

Content:
- When calculating the product [MATH: A^T \mathbf x,] we multiply each row of [MATH: A^T] by [MATH: \mathbf x.]
- Suppose that [MATH: \mathbf x\in \text{Null}(A^T).] Then, by definition, [MATH: A^T \mathbf x = \mathbf 0.]
- Thus, [MATH: \mathbf x] must be orthogonal to each row of [MATH: A^T.] Equivalently, this means that [MATH: \mathbf x] is orthogonal to each column of [MATH: A.]
- Hence, [MATH: \text{Null}(A^T)] is orthogonal to [MATH: \text{Col}(A).]

Content:
We can deduce that [MATH: \text{Null}(A)] is the orthogonal complement of [MATH: \text{Col}(A^T)] by similar reasoning.

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying an Orthogonal Fundamental Subspaces of a Matrix

Example Prompt:
Which of the following subspaces must be orthogonal to [MATH: \text{Col}(A^T)] for every matrix [MATH: A?]

1. [MATH: \text{Null}(A)]
2. [MATH: \text{Col}(A)]
3. [MATH: \text{Null}(A^T)]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that [MATH: \text{Col}(A^T)] is the row space of [MATH: A,] and consists of all linear combinations of the rows of [MATH: A.]

If a vector is orthogonal to every linear combination of the rows of [MATH: A,] it must be orthogonal to each row of [MATH: A.]
But notice that when pre-multiplying a vector by [MATH: A,] we multiply each row of [MATH: A] by that vector.
So, [MATH: \text{Col}(A^T)] must be orthogonal to the null space of [MATH: A,] which is [MATH: \text{Null}(A).]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Note: In general, the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix [MATH: A] can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/3f5d3f205e1bbfefa33c962c08289313]

---

3. [MATH: Col(A)]

Choices:
a. III only
b. II only
c. I only
d. II and III only
e. I and III only

Item 5 — Tutorial: Images Under the Action of a Matrix and Its Transpose

Content:
Given an [MATH: m \times n] matrix [MATH: A,] what is the image of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] under [MATH: A?]

Content:
Note that pre-multiplying a vector [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n] by [MATH: A] gives a linear combination of the columns of [MATH: A{:}]
[MATH: [||||⋯||; a_{1}|a_{2}|⋯|a_{n};||||⋯||]]

Content:
Therefore, by definition, the image of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] under the action of [MATH: A] is [MATH: \text{Col}(A),] the column space of [MATH: A.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fd819e94aa13fdf60f90e01c4669cca7]

Content:
Similarly, pre-multiplying a vector [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^m] by [MATH: A^T] gives a linear combination of the columns of [MATH: A^T{:}]
[MATH: [||||⋯||; a_{1}^{T}|a_{2}^{T}|⋯|a_{m}^{T};||||⋯||]]

Content:
Therefore, the image of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^m] under the action of [MATH: A^T] must be [MATH: \text{Col}(A^T).] This is also the row space of [MATH: A,] since a linear combination of the columns of [MATH: A^T] is equivalent to a linear combination of the rows of [MATH: A.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/46bf86653ce6e6d460ef48eca5975949]

Content:
We can use similar reasoning to find the image of the four fundamental subspaces under the appropriate matrix.

---

Item 6 — Example: Identifying the Images of the Four Fundamental Subspaces of the Matrix Under Its Action

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: A] be a [MATH: m \times n] matrix. What is the image of [MATH: \text{Col}(A^T)] under the action of [MATH: A?]

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Pre-multiplying a vector [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n] by [MATH: A] gives a linear combination of the columns of [MATH: A{:}]

[MATH: [||||⋯||; a_{1}|a_{2}|⋯|a_{n};||||⋯||]]

Therefore, the image of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] under the action of [MATH: A] must be [MATH: \text{Col}(A),] the column space of [MATH: A.]

Furthermore, since [MATH: \text{Null}(A)] is mapped to the zero vector [MATH: \mathbf{0}] by the definition of the null subspace, the image of its orthogonal complement [MATH: \text{Col}(A^T)] must be [MATH: \text{Col}(A).]

This can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/8316316663e36bb3df40f825362d5116]

- [MATH: \text{dim}(\text{Null}(A^T)) = m-r.] Since [MATH: \text{Null}(A^T)] is the orthogonal complement of [MATH: \text{Col}(A)] in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^m,] we have that

- the image of [MATH: \text{Col}(A)] under the action of [MATH: A^T] is [MATH: \text{Col}(A^T).]
